news.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, with cheaper Astra pricing and new risk ratings
news.summary: Astra targets demanding work in science, law and finance and now costs $8/$40 per million input/output tokens, about 20% less than before; Sol stays at $2/$10 for everyday tasks. OpenAI rates both 'Critical' for cybersecurity, and says Astra is the first model it has released that reaches 'High' for AI self-improvement.

news.title: Nvidia posts $115.8B quarter and guides to $130B in its first report since Huang's exit
news.summary: Revenue doubled year on year, with data center sales at $107.6B, and Vera Rubin NVL72 systems have started shipping. The Q4 outlook of $130B (plus or minus 3%) assumes no data center compute revenue from China; interim CEO Colette Kress led the report while the board searches for a permanent chief.

news.title: Microsoft uses Ignite to launch in-house MAI coding and security models plus Maia 300
news.summary: New MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash coding models are generally available in GitHub Copilot and Foundry, alongside a Cyber 2 Flash security model and a 'Licensed Weights' option for trusted customers. Microsoft also unveiled its Maia 300 chip and expanded Agent 365, a control plane it says already manages over 50 million agents.

news.title: Anthropic likely to price its IPO above the $70-$78 range
news.summary: Sources told CNBC the offering is likely to price above its marketed range, after reports that orders reached about six times the 825 million shares on offer. Final pricing is expected Wednesday, with Nasdaq trading set to start on November 19.

news.title: Robotics startup Genesis AI raises $500M at a $3.5B valuation
news.summary: Khosla Ventures, Premji Invest and Eclipse co-led the Paris-based company's Series A, with Nvidia and AMD's venture arms joining. The money will put its two-armed, wheeled Eno robots into factories and warehouses, with mass production at a US contract manufacturer due next year.

news.title: Cognition launches Devin Bots, persistent agents that manage teams of coding agents
news.summary: A Devin Bot splits a long software project into tasks, assigns them to Devin sessions, keeps context for weeks and pings humans in Slack when it is blocked. Cognition says early-access usage grew tenfold in two weeks, and pitches it against OpenAI's Dots and Anthropic's Duet.

news.title: Replit Missions sends a swarm of agents after a goal, within a spending cap
news.summary: Users set a goal, a budget and which actions need sign-off; agents plan, build and test while an independent AI judge checks results against agreed criteria. Replit says Missions built an app-monitoring platform, now open-sourced, in two days for under $3,000.

news.title: ElevenLabs to acquire Japanese voice AI lab Kotoba
news.summary: Kotoba's Koto model handles Japanese speech recognition, speech synthesis and simultaneous interpretation, and already powers Japanese conversations in Salesforce's Agentforce Voice. ElevenLabs plans to hire locally and invest in Japanese infrastructure; the deal should close this quarter, pending approvals.

news.title: Google starts converting Gemini Gems into skills
news.summary: From November 17, personal accounts' custom and shared Gems are automatically migrated to skills, which users call up with a slash in the chat and can combine. Skills require the Keep Activity setting, and Workspace business accounts follow in March 2027.

papers.title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration
papers.tldr: Humanoid robots trained in pairs learn to carry out long shared jobs as teams of up to ten, each acting on its own senses and syncing by spoken cues instead of a network.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
Heave-Ho lets a team of humanoid robots carry out long, shared physical jobs together, such as moving a heavy object, with each robot deciding for itself and no network link between them.

## Background you need
A humanoid is a robot with a human-like body: two legs, two arms and a torso. Loco-manipulation means walking and using your hands at the same time, like carrying a box across a room. A foundation tracking model is a large pretrained controller that makes a robot's body follow a target motion. A decentralized system is one where every robot acts on its own view of the world, without a central computer giving orders.

## The problem
Some jobs are too big for one robot. Lifting a long table, or pushing a heavy cart, needs several bodies working in step. This is hard for three reasons. First, the robots are physically linked through the object, so one robot's push changes what the others feel. Second, the job has many stages, so someone has to plan them. Third, timing matters: if one robot lifts early, the load tips. Most existing systems rely on a central planner or a constant wireless link. Those are fragile in the real world, where networks drop out and robots break.

## The idea
The authors split the job into two layers, a bit like a team of movers. The movers' bodies know how to lift and walk while feeling the shared weight. One mover acts as the leader and calls out "lift!" or "walk!" out loud. The others hear the call and act. Nobody needs a radio; they only need eyes, ears and a sense of the load.

## How it works
1. **Start from a strong body controller.** The team takes an existing humanoid foundation tracking model, which already knows how to move a single robot's body.
2. **Post-train it for teamwork.** They add multi-agent post-training: extra training in simulation where several robots handle the same object. Each robot learns to act from its own local observations only, and to cope with the pushes and pulls that come through the shared object.
3. **Plan with a vision-language model.** At the high level, a vision-language planner (an AI model that reads camera images and text) breaks the long task into stages.
4. **Sync by speech.** A leader-follower scheme uses spoken commands so the robots switch stages at the same moment, without any network messages.
5. **Train small, deploy big.** Training uses just two identical humanoids. The same system is then used with larger teams and with mixed teams of different robot types, without retraining.

## Results
The paper reports that a system trained with two robots scales to teams of up to ten humanoids. It also transfers to heterogeneous teams (robots of different designs) with no extra training. That matters because collecting training data for every team size and mix would be very costly.

The authors also built HH-Bench, a test suite of 12 tasks with teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including mixed teams. On it, they report that Heave-Ho beats the baseline methods consistently. Real-world experiments show the robots collaborating on hard tasks without central control. The summary available to us does not give the exact success rates, so we do not quote them here.

## Why it matters
Warehouses, construction sites and disaster zones are full of loads too big for one machine. A team that coordinates by voice and local sensing keeps working when Wi-Fi fails. Training once with two robots and then growing the team also cuts the cost of deployment. For researchers, HH-Bench gives a shared yardstick for multi-humanoid work, which has been hard to compare so far.

## Caveats
Speech-based syncing could struggle in loud places, such as a factory floor. The number of robots tested tops out at ten. The high-level plan depends on a vision-language model, which can misread scenes. The headline comparison is on a benchmark the authors themselves created, so independent tests would help. Long-term reliability and hardware wear were not the focus.

## Key terms
- **Humanoid:** a robot shaped roughly like a person.
- **Loco-manipulation:** moving around and handling objects at the same time.
- **Decentralized control:** each robot decides using only what it senses, with no central boss.
- **Post-training:** extra training that adapts an already-trained model to a new skill.
- **Vision-language planner:** an AI model that looks at images and reads text to decide the next step.
- **Leader-follower:** one robot signals stage changes and the others follow its cue.

papers.title: Lost in a Few Heads: Diagnosing and Repairing Block Selection in Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: Sparse-attention models that lose facts in long documents are usually let down by a few 'blind' attention heads; patching only those heads lifts retrieval from 54% to 97.5% while keeping most of the speedup.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The paper finds that when "sparse attention" models forget a key fact in a long document, the fault usually lies with a handful of attention heads, and fixing just those heads restores almost all the lost accuracy without any retraining.

## Background you need
Large language models read text with attention: for each new word, the model looks back over earlier words to decide what matters. Attention is split across many heads, small parallel "readers" that each look for different patterns. With long inputs, full attention gets slow, so sparse attention lets each query read only a fixed budget of key blocks (chunks of earlier text). A block selector decides which blocks to read, usually by comparing the query with a short summary of each block.

## The problem
Sparse attention saves time on long documents, but accuracy can drop sharply. The classic test is "needle in a haystack": hide one fact in a huge text and ask for it later. Sparse models often miss the needle. The natural guess is that the reading budget is too small. If that were true, the only fix would be to read more blocks, which gives back the speed savings. That matters for anyone running chatbots over long contracts, codebases or chat histories.

## The idea
The authors show the budget is usually not the problem. The selector ranks the needle's block too low. Think of a librarian who skims a one-line summary of each shelf. If the summary is an average of every book on the shelf, one crucial book gets drowned out. The authors find that only a few "blind" heads suffer this way. These heads do want to look at the needle, but the averaged block summary hides it.

## How it works
1. **Diagnose.** They run a calibration probe, a short test that checks, head by head, whether the selector keeps or drops the blocks that hold the answer.
2. **Find the blind heads.** They propose one rule that flags heads where the needle's block is under-ranked. The culprit is mean-pooling: averaging all keys in a block, which dilutes the single token that decides the answer.
3. **Fix option A.** Give only the flagged heads full attention, so they read everything. All other heads stay sparse.
4. **Fix option B.** Keep the same budget, but score blocks with a 4-bit scorer, a cheap, low-precision way to compare the query with the actual keys instead of their average.
5. **No training.** Both fixes are applied at inference time to existing models.

## Results
On MiniCPM4.1-8B with 64K-token inputs, multi-key retrieval accuracy rises from 54.1% to 97.5% with either fix, matching full attention. In plain terms, a model that found the facts about half the time now finds them almost always.

On Qwen3-8B with SeerAttention-R gates, giving full attention to 18 of 288 key-value heads (about 6%) lifts accuracy from 29.8% to 97.7%.

Speed is mostly kept. In production serving engines, the fixed models retain 84–89% of the time-to-first-token savings (how long before the first word of a reply appears) that sparse attention gives at 32K–128K context. The same few-heads pattern shows up across InfLLM-V2, NOSA, SeerAttention-R, NSA and DashAttention. MoBA is the exception, with many more problem heads.

## Why it matters
Teams serving long-context models can recover accuracy with a small, targeted patch instead of abandoning sparse attention. It also changes how sparse attention should be designed: block summaries that average everything are the weak point. Better summaries, or per-head budgets, are a clear next step.

## Caveats
Results focus on retrieval-style tests; harder reasoning over long text may behave differently. The probe needs calibration data, and flagged heads could shift for new tasks. MoBA did not show the same neat pattern, so the fix is not universal. Some speed is still lost compared with fully sparse decoding.

## Key terms
- **Attention head:** one of many parallel sub-readers inside a model's attention layer.
- **Sparse attention:** reading only a chosen subset of earlier text blocks to save time.
- **Block selector:** the component that decides which blocks each head reads.
- **Mean-pooling:** summarizing a block by averaging its contents.
- **Time-to-first-token:** the wait before a model starts its reply.
- **4-bit scorer:** a low-precision, cheap way to compute relevance scores.

papers.title: Communicate the Change: Efficient Expert Parallelism via Activation Compression
papers.tldr: EchoMoE sends only the compressed change in each token's state between machines, cutting mixture-of-experts network traffic by 58% and boosting throughput up to 2.38x on Ethernet.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
EchoMoE makes huge "mixture-of-experts" language models run faster across many machines by sending only the compressed change in each token's internal state, instead of the full state.

## Background you need
A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model contains many small sub-networks called experts, and each token (a word piece) is sent to only a few of them. This gives a model lots of knowledge without doing all the math for every token. When a model is too big for one machine, its experts are spread across devices; this is expert parallelism. The residual stream is the running internal "notes" for each token that every layer reads and slightly updates.

## The problem
With experts on different machines, every MoE layer has two forced pauses. First, each token's state is shipped to the machines holding its experts. Then the results are shipped back. These are collective communication steps, and every device must wait for them. Computer chips have become much faster, but the cables between machines have not kept up. So these transfers are now a major bottleneck, especially on cheaper networks such as Ethernet. Slower transfers mean slower, pricier replies for every user.

## The idea
A transformer changes each token's notes only a little from layer to layer. So most of what gets shipped is old news. EchoMoE is like a newsroom sending only the edits to a story instead of reprinting the whole paper each hour. Both sides keep a copy of an earlier version, called a reference, and only the difference travels.

## How it works
1. **Keep a reference.** The hidden state from an earlier layer is stored on both the sender and receiver side.
2. **Compute the change.** At the current layer, the model subtracts the reference from the current hidden state to get the difference.
3. **Compress and send.** That difference is compressed into a smaller form and sent over the network. The paper reports this also tolerates quantized (lower-precision) messages without a measurable quality loss.
4. **Refresh now and then.** References are refreshed periodically so the differences stay small and errors do not build up.
5. **Retrofit, do not retrain.** The change is added to existing pretrained MoE models with a short adaptation run. The authors report about 8,500 times fewer training tokens than full pretraining. They release code, Qwen3-30B-A3B checkpoints and a vLLM integration (vLLM is a popular serving engine).

## Results
EchoMoE cuts inter-node traffic by 58%, so less than half the data now crosses the network. Throughput, the number of tokens served per second, rises by 22.6% overall. On bandwidth-limited Ethernet setups, inference throughput improves by up to 2.38 times. In practice, a cluster that served 100 replies a minute could serve about 238.

Quality drops a little. Across 18 benchmarks, average performance stays within 3.8 percentage points of the original model. The comparison is against the same model running standard expert parallelism.

## Why it matters
Cloud providers and companies running open MoE models pay heavily for fast interconnects. A software change that lets cheaper networks keep up could lower the cost of serving large models. Because it is a retrofit with low training cost, teams can try it on models they already use rather than training from scratch.

## Caveats
A gap of up to 3.8 points is noticeable for some uses, and it may vary by task. The biggest gains appear when the network is the bottleneck; on very fast links the benefit shrinks. The method needs some extra training, and the released checkpoints cover one model family. Extra memory for storing references is a cost worth checking at scale.

## Key terms
- **Mixture-of-experts (MoE):** a model that routes each token to a few specialist sub-networks.
- **Expert parallelism:** spreading those experts across many machines.
- **Residual stream:** the running internal state each layer reads and updates.
- **Collective communication:** a step where all devices exchange data and wait for each other.
- **Throughput:** how much work a system finishes per second.
- **Quantization:** storing numbers with fewer bits to save space and bandwidth.

papers.title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
papers.tldr: In mixture-of-experts diffusion language models the word-sampling step, not the experts, is the main bottleneck; fused GPU kernels for it make decoding 2.4-2.7x faster with no accuracy loss.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors discover that a "boring" bookkeeping step, picking words from the model's scores, eats most of the time in a fast new kind of language model, and they rewrite it as GPU code that makes the whole model 2.4–2.7 times faster.

## Background you need
Most chatbots write one word at a time. Diffusion language models work differently: they start with a canvas of blank slots and fill and refine many words at once over several passes. Each pass produces logits, the model's raw score for every possible word in every slot. A sampler turns those scores into chosen words and decides which slots are confident enough to lock in. A GPU kernel is a small program that runs on the graphics chip; fusing kernels means doing several steps in one program to avoid slow trips to memory.

## The problem
People usually assume the heavy math inside the model is what makes it slow. In mixture-of-experts models, that math is the experts' matrix multiplications (GEMMs). So engineers quantize the weights (store them in fewer bits) to speed them up. But a diffusion model re-scores the whole canvas on every pass. The sampler therefore runs over a giant table of scores again and again. On small "edge" devices, that hidden cost can dominate. It makes local, private AI on a desk-side box slower than it should be.

## The idea
Profile first, then fix the real bottleneck. It is like a kitchen that buys faster ovens, only to learn that the waiters are the hold-up. Once the experts were quantized, the sampling pipeline, not the experts, was the single biggest time sink.

## How it works
1. **Measure.** They profile one user decoding with a 26-billion-parameter diffusion MoE model on an NVIDIA GB10, a compact accelerator with 273 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
2. **Bit-exact tier.** They remove waste from the existing sampling steps while producing output that matches the reference decoder byte for byte. This is safe for anyone who needs identical results.
3. **Accuracy-parity tier.** They go further with a fused single-pass entropy kernel. Entropy measures how unsure the model is about each slot, and the kernel computes it in one sweep over the scores. They also use Gumbel-max sampling, a trick that picks a random word with the right odds by adding noise and taking the maximum, avoiding extra passes.
4. **Speed up the experts too.** They pair this with a W4A16 expert kernel: weights in 4 bits, activations in 16 bits.
5. **Check generality.** They repeat the study on a second diffusion MoE and on a dense (non-expert) diffusion model.

## Results
The full stack runs 2.4–2.7 times faster than the standard 16-bit (bf16) version on one device. A reply that took 10 seconds now takes about 4. Accuracy on GSM8K (grade-school math), HumanEval (coding) and MATH is unchanged.

On a second model, LLaDA2.0-mini, the sampling pipeline takes 28.8% of decode time, and the fused W4A16 version is 3.3 times faster at matching accuracy. On a dense diffusion model, the pipeline takes only 3.6% of decode time. So this bottleneck is specific to mixture-of-experts diffusion models. Code and quantized weights are released.

## Why it matters
Diffusion language models are a promising route to faster text generation. This work shows that their speed depends on the "glue" code as much as the model. Anyone deploying them on laptops or small servers can get large gains without changing the model itself. It is also a reminder to profile before optimizing.

## Caveats
Tests focus on a single user on one edge device; big data-center GPUs with many users may see different bottlenecks. Only two MoE diffusion models were studied. The faster tier matches benchmark accuracy but is not byte-identical, which may matter for some audits.

## Key terms
- **Diffusion language model:** a model that fills in many words at once over repeated passes.
- **Logits:** raw scores a model gives each possible word.
- **Sampler:** the code that turns scores into chosen words.
- **GPU kernel:** a small program that runs on the graphics chip.
- **Quantization (W4A16):** storing weights in 4 bits while keeping activations in 16 bits.
- **Gumbel-max:** a fast trick for random sampling with the right probabilities.

papers.title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters
papers.tldr: Putting a 552-billion-parameter model behind a robot controller lets it learn from 10 demonstrations instead of 50 and plug in a charger 9 times out of 10 instead of 4.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
ScaleVLA plugs a giant 552-billion-parameter AI model into a robot controller and shows that bigger "brains" help robots learn from fewer examples, cope with new situations and do fiddly tasks like plugging in a charger.

## Background you need
A vision-language-action (VLA) model is a robot policy, the software that decides the robot's next move, built from a model that understands images and text. Its backbone is the large pretrained model that does the seeing and reading. A demonstration is a recording of a person guiding the robot through a task. An action chunk is a short sequence of planned robot moves produced in one go.

## The problem
Today's robot policies mostly use small backbones, often a few billion parameters. Frontier language models are hundreds of times bigger and know far more about the world. Robot builders have avoided them because they are slow and costly. So no one knew whether that extra knowledge would actually help a robot's hands. Meanwhile, every robot task still needs dozens of costly human demonstrations, and robots often fail when a scene looks slightly different.

## The idea
Treat the frontier model as the robot's well-read brain and add a small, trainable "motor cortex" on top. It is like hiring a seasoned expert who has read every manual and pairing them with a new apprentice's hands. The question is simple: with everything else held equal, does a bigger brain make better hands?

## How it works
1. **Pick a huge backbone.** The team uses DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, a 552-billion-parameter model, to process camera images and instructions.
2. **Add an action head.** A trainable action diffusion transformer turns the backbone's understanding into robot motions. Diffusion here means it refines a noisy guess of the motion into a clean one.
3. **Compare fairly.** They train backbones from 2 billion to 552 billion parameters under one shared recipe, so size is the main difference.
4. **Test three skills.** They measure sample efficiency (learning from few demos), generalization (handling changed scenes) and precise manipulation on a real robot.
5. **Keep it usable.** They measure latency, the time to produce each action chunk.

## Results
Sample efficiency: with only 10 demonstrations, the 552B model succeeds 87.8% of the time, beating a 2B backbone trained on 50 demonstrations (85.6%). That is one-fifth of the human teaching effort for slightly better results.

Generalization: on LIBERO-PRO, a test with altered tasks and scenes, the large model reaches 45.1% success. Smaller backbones top out at 31.3%.

Precision: on a real robot inserting a charger, successes rise from 4 out of 10 to 9 out of 10. The biggest gains come in contact-sensitive alignment, the final millimeters where the plug meets the socket.

Speed: median latency is 216 milliseconds per action chunk, fast enough for many table-top tasks despite the size.

## Why it matters
Teaching robots is expensive, and fewer demonstrations means cheaper deployment of new tasks. The work suggests that progress in frontier language models can flow directly into better robot skills. Robotics labs may now treat giant models as foundations for control, not only as high-level planners.

## Caveats
Running a 552B model needs serious computing hardware, which most robots cannot carry. The precision test uses 10 trials, a small sample. Even the best generalization score, 45.1%, means the robot still fails more than half the time on changed scenes. Results come from one backbone family, so other large models may behave differently.

## Key terms
- **VLA model:** a robot controller built on a model that understands images and language.
- **Backbone:** the large pretrained model doing perception and understanding.
- **Demonstration:** a recorded example of a person showing the robot a task.
- **Action diffusion transformer:** a network that refines rough motion guesses into precise actions.
- **Latency:** the delay between seeing and acting.
- **LIBERO-PRO:** a test suite of robot tasks with changed conditions to check generalization.

papers.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
papers.tldr: China Telecom details how it trained agent-focused Xing 4 models entirely on Huawei Ascend chips, including a 285B model on 8,192 cards, plus a training gym that keeps chips busy during agent RL.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
China Telecom's lab explains how it built Xing 4, a family of agent-focused language models trained entirely on Huawei's Ascend chips instead of Nvidia GPUs, including a 285-billion-parameter model trained on 8,192 chips.

## Background you need
A large language model (LLM) is trained in two phases. Pretraining teaches it language from huge amounts of text. Post-training then shapes it for useful work, often with reinforcement learning (RL), where the model tries tasks and is rewarded for good results. An agentic model is one built to plan steps and call tools, such as running code or searching. Ascend is Huawei's family of AI chips, and MindSpore is Huawei's software framework for training on them.

## The problem
US export rules limit access to top Nvidia chips in China. Chinese labs therefore need to train frontier models on domestic hardware. That is hard: the software tools are younger, and tricks tuned for Nvidia do not carry over. Agent training adds another headache. An agent must run long tasks in real software environments, and slow tasks can leave expensive chips sitting idle while they wait.

## The idea
The report treats the model, the chips and the training system as one design problem. Think of a car maker forced to use a new engine: you redesign the body, the gearbox and the assembly line together, not just swap the engine. The same goes for the agent training loop. The team built a single "gym" where task execution, scoring and learning run side by side, so no part waits on another.

## How it works
1. **Design the model for efficiency.** The report covers sparse activation (only part of the model works on each token, as in mixture-of-experts), attention design, the balance of depth and width, and speculative decoding (a small guesser drafts tokens that the big model checks).
2. **Scale pretraining on Ascend.** Using the MindSpore HyperParallel stack, they pretrain a 285-billion-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards.
3. **Build TeleGym.** This platform links running agent tasks, grading them and turning the runs into training data for the policy (the model being trained).
4. **Keep chips busy.** TeleGym uses disaggregated asynchronous execution: task running and learning happen on separate machines and do not wait for each other. Bounded oversampling launches a few extra attempts, capped, so slow ones do not stall a batch. Partial rollout lets long tasks be paused and resumed across training steps.

## Results
The report's main result is feasibility at scale: a 285B model pretrained across 8,192 domestic chips.

A released family member, Xing4.0-29B-A4B (29 billion parameters, 4 billion active per token), gives a sense of quality. Its model card, written by the developer, reports 75.0 on SWE-bench Verified (fixing real code bugs) and 57.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (command-line tasks). For comparison, it lists Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at 76.0 and 51.5, and Gemma4-26B-A4B at 53.0 and 30.0. So it is roughly level with a leading open rival of similar size. The card also says training throughput rose about 96% over the chips' default performance after tuning.

## Why it matters
This is evidence that competitive agent models can be trained without Nvidia hardware. That affects chip export policy, supply chains and the global spread of open models. TeleGym's design ideas, such as not letting slow tasks block learning, apply to any lab doing agent RL.

## Caveats
Benchmark numbers come from the developers, with settings that may differ between models. The summary we could read does not give full scores for the 285B model, so its quality versus top Western models is unclear. Much of the engineering is specific to Huawei's stack and may not transfer elsewhere.

## Key terms
- **Pretraining / post-training:** first learning language broadly, then tuning for useful behavior.
- **Reinforcement learning:** learning by trial, with rewards for good outcomes.
- **Sparse activation:** using only part of the model for each token to save compute.
- **Speculative decoding:** a small model drafts text that the large model quickly verifies.
- **Rollout:** one full attempt by an agent at a task, used as training data.
- **Ascend 910C:** a Huawei AI chip used here instead of Nvidia GPUs.
